<reflection>
- The previous experiment (low S, high cat) successfully shifted the model rankings, bringing several catalyst deactivation models (M20, M11, M14, M9) to the top. However, the NLL differences remain extremely small (less than 1 log-likelihood unit separates the top 10 models). 
- My aim to break the degeneracy was only partially achieved. The models can still mimic each other because we have not yet tested the catalyst's long-term stability. In all previous runs, the catalyst concentration was relatively high (0.05 to 0.20), meaning the reaction could reach completion (or near completion) before significant deactivation occurred.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To definitively separate the deactivation mechanisms from standard Michaelis-Menten (M1) and from each other, we must force the system into a "high turnover" regime. I propose an experiment with the maximum substrate concentration (S=5.0) and a very low catalyst concentration (cat=0.005).
1. In this regime, the catalyst must undergo 1,000 turnover cycles to fully convert the substrate. Models without deactivation (M1, M2, M5) will eventually reach full conversion, whereas deactivation models (M9, M11, M14, M20) will stall prematurely, leaving a massive, undeniable gap in the predicted final product concentration.
2. Because the substrate concentration is so high, the catalyst will be heavily saturated, existing almost entirely as the `catS` complex. This will strongly differentiate the *type* of deactivation: models where the `catS` complex deactivates (M14) will stall very quickly, whereas models where free `cat` deactivates (M9) will be "protected" by the high substrate concentration and will deactivate much more slowly.
3. Starting with zero product (P=0.0) allows us to observe the natural accumulation of product over a long period. Models with product-induced deactivation (M12, M17) will show a unique accelerating deactivation curve as P builds up from 0 to 5.0, distinguishing them from first-order deactivation models.
</hypothesis>
